What I mean by this is that it seems like most hard modes seem to ether do 1 of two things. Just give the player less health (which is fine when the standard difficulty is piss easy), or make it so the player does less damage which just makes things tedious and not actually harder. Also games sometimes require the player to unlock higher difficulties which just feels like padding.

There are a few examples I can think of. The first is the knuckles run of sonic 3. Which not only gives you a character that plays slightly different (IE slower and can't jump as high as sonic but can glide, climb walls, and punch through walls instead of just needing to spin dash) but also forces you through harder pathways.

The second example is most old school shooters. Basically they change where and when enemies spawn based on the difficulty which is solid design
What are games that actually do higher difficulties properly

Rewards are shit though. Like there's no reason to play Expert over Normal mode when some items can't even be used in Normal mode. The items you get in Expert mode are also shit.
For one the challenge, and two the rewards are greatly increased.
It's really just for the challenge, the vast majority of the expert mode drops except for the ones from the first few bosses are complete ass.

the XCOMs

(worthy mention - Killing Floor 2, where the increase in difficulty changes many aspects of the game play, notably enemy behavior)
xcom does it right because enemy health actually affects strategy, which is an important difference.

Devil May Cry games. Not only do enemies get more health and do more damage as you progress through the difficulties, they become more aggressive and coordinate attacks with other enemies, and can enter a Devil Trigger (for those that are unfamiliar with the game, it's a sort of hyper-damage, no-stagger, health regen transformation the player can use for a limited time) state if not dealt with in a timely enough manner.

Oh and if you master that mode, there's also an additional mode that builds on that difficulty and adds "everything except bosses dies in one hit that means enemies and the player."

High difficulty levels can sometimes be tedious (think Skyrim) because the game just asks you to do the same thing as you did before, but longer. In other cases and mostly in strategy games, high difficulty pins you into one strategy that exploits game mechanics to the maximum without being actually fun to implement (i.e. no choices are difficult to make). Difficulty levels done right require you to do the same thing better, faster and using fewer resources. Simply upping the simulation speed of any action game will make it harder, but that's often a bad choice because it tends to break human reaction time limits, controller precision and all these kinds of things.

As for a game that does this properly, I kind of think Europa Universalis IV does this right by letting you chose any country. And there is no silver bullet strategy to win in this game, although some choices clearly work much better than others.

high difficulty pins you into one strategy that exploits game mechanics to the maximum without being actually fun to implement

4X games do that so hard.
Mass Effect 2 insanity difficulty, enemies are stronger and have bigger health bars and are more aggressive, while two gun fire burst can kill you and your squadmates drop pretty fast as well.

Doing difficulties properly, in my opinion is something that changes the way you play. This means doing it bad is usually "number of mistakes you can make". While the good is usually "how hard it is to avoid getting mistakes".

A lot of bullet hell games do difficulties right. Examples include Touhou, Jamestown and many Cave shoot'em ups. In these games, it's the bullet patterns which get more and more complicated and harder-to-avoid.

Crysis on Delta difficulty changes the game mechanics in interesting ways. Firstly, enemies will only speak Korean and without subtitles so you don't know what they are saying. Enemies are no longer automatically shown on the mini map and must be tagged with your binoculars before they appear there, for example. Little features that are changed in ways that make sense and make the game harder and more immersive. I could go so far as to say that if you didn't play it on Delta you were playing a different game.

Not to mention Crysis games on really high difficulty make it so that you die in like 3 or 4 hits. In some games I think that's super annoying, but I liked it since it actually forced you to play the game like a predator.

Particularly the hardest difficulty of 3.

I'm not sure this answers your question, but From Software has figured hard games out. If you haven't played Demon's/Dark Souls or Bloodborne, give it a shot. The games are not terribly complex, but it is extremely satisfying to beat a boss without taking damage because you know the moves and got the timing right. These games lend themselves to self challenge well, meaning, you can increase the difficulty by playing a little differently, or trying different gear.

The difficulty of Dark Souls is one of the fairest difficulties in modern games, IMO. Yes, it's pretty difficult, but the difficulty comes from you having not discovered how to exploit an enemy's weakest point yet, rather than just because they have too much health or do too much damage.
I was put off at first because the controls aren't "tight". What I found is the controls are actually very precise and repeatable. Dark Souls 2 is definitely a masochist's game.

I really liked Far Cry 3 on hard mode. I was about a third of my way through the game playing normal and I heard on reddit to try hard to make it interesting. I did, and then the whole way I approached the game changed. When an enemy patrol is passing by, instead of just killing everyone I had to hide, and hunting got more intense. Taking bases also became much more strategic with a lot of trial and error.
